bio.en: Sherwin Wu is Head of Engineering for OpenAI's API and Developer Platform, giving him a uniquely broad view into the AI startup ecosystem since nearly every AI company integrates with OpenAI's APIs.
bio.zh: Sherwin Wu 是 OpenAI API 与开发者平台工程负责人，由于几乎每一家 AI 公司都接入 OpenAI 的 API，这让他对 AI 创业生态拥有极其独特而广博的视野。

summary.en: Sherwin discusses what he sees across the thousands of teams building on OpenAI's APIs, from common architectural patterns to the mistakes that sink AI products. He shares how developers should think about evaluation, reliability, and cost as models and agents become more capable, and where the platform is heading. The episode is a rare, behind-the-API look at the state and future of AI application development.
summary.zh: Sherwin 讨论了他在数千支基于 OpenAI API 构建的团队中所观察到的现象，从常见的架构模式，到拖垮 AI 产品的那些错误。他分享了随着模型与智能体能力增强，开发者应如何思考评估、可靠性与成本，以及平台的前进方向。本期是一份难得的、API 背后的 AI 应用开发现状与未来透视。

turns.en: 95% of engineers use Codex. 100% of our PRs are reviewed by Codex.

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: For engineers, I don't know what job has changed more in the past couple years.
turns.zh: 对于工程师来说，我不知道过去几年里哪个岗位的变化最大。

turns.speaker: Sherwin Wu
turns.en: Engineers are becoming tech leads. They're managing fleets and fleets of agents. It literally feels like we're wizards casting all these spells and these spells are kind of like going out and doing things for you.
turns.zh: 工程师们正在成为技术负责人。他们管理着大量代理团队。感觉我们简直就像魔法师，在施展各种法术，而这些法术又像是外出为你办事。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What do you think people aren't pricing in yet?
turns.zh: 你觉得人们目前还没有考虑到哪些因素？

turns.speaker: Sherwin Wu
turns.en: The second or third order effects of the one person billion dollar startup. To enable a one person billion dollar startup, there might be a hundred other small startups building bespoke software. So I think we might actually enter into a golden age of B2B SaaS.
turns.zh: 单人亿级美元初创公司的二阶或三阶效应。要实现单人亿级美元初创公司，可能需要数百家其他小型初创公司开发定制软件。所以我认为我们可能真的会迎来B2B SaaS的黄金时代。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I've been hearing more and more there's this stress people feel when their agents aren't working.
turns.zh: 我越来越听说人们因为代理无法正常工作而感到压力很大。

turns.speaker: Sherwin Wu
turns.en: There's a team that's actually doing an experiment right now within OpenAI where they are maintaining a 100% Codex-written code base. They run into the exact problems that you're describing. And so usually you're like, "All right, I'll roll up my sleeves and figure it out." This team doesn't have that escape hatch.
turns.zh: OpenAI内部有一个团队正在进行实验，他们维护着一个100%由Codex编写的代码库。他们遇到了你所描述的那些问题。而通常情况下，你可能会想，"好吧，我会卷起袖子把问题解决。"但这个团队没有退路。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: You've shared that. Listening to customers is not always the right strategy in AI.
turns.zh: 你提到过这一点。对于AI来说，倾听客户意见并不总是正确的策略。

turns.speaker: Sherwin Wu
turns.en: The field and the models themselves are just changing so, so quickly. They tend to disrupt themselves. The models will eat your scaffolding for breakfast.
turns.zh: 这个领域和模型本身变化得非常快。它们往往会自我颠覆。模型会把你的框架当作早餐吃掉。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What's your advice to folks that are like, "Okay, I don't want to miss the boat."
turns.zh: 对于那些想"好吧，我不想错过这波浪潮"的人，你有什么建议？

turns.speaker: Sherwin Wu
turns.en: Make sure you're building for where the models are going and not where they are today. There's a quote from Kevin Weil, our VP of science here, and he likes saying, "This is the worst the models will ever be."
turns.zh: 确保你是在为模型未来的发展方向而构建，而不是为它们当前的状态而构建。这里有句话来自我们的科学副总裁Kevin Weil，他常说："这将是模型表现最差的时期。"

turns.en: I want to start with what's feeling like a barometer of progress in AI, especially in engineering. What percentage of your code, if you even write code anymore, and your team's code is written by AI at this point?
turns.zh: 首先我想谈谈AI在工程领域的进展指标，特别是从工程角度来看。请问您现在编写的代码（如果您还写代码的话），以及您团队的代码中，有多大比例是由AI生成的？

turns.speaker: Sherwin Wu
turns.en: I do write code occasionally now still. And I'd actually say for managers like myself, it's way easier to use these AI tools than to manually code at this point. And so I know for myself and some of the other EMs, engineering managers at OpenAI, all of our code is written by Codex at this point. But more broadly, there's just so much energy. There's a tangible energy internally around just how far these tools have gotten, how good Codex as a tool has gotten for us. And it's a little hard for us to exactly measure how much of the code is written because the vast majority of it, I'd say close to 100% is usually generated by AI first. What we do track though is at this point, the vast majority of engineers use Codex on a daily basis. So 95% of engineers use Codex. (00:04:21): 100% of our PRs are reviewed by Codex daily as well. So basically any code that goes into production that's merged in, Codex kind of has its eyes on and suggests improvements, suggests changes in the PRs. And so that's kind of what we're seeing internally, but by and large, the most exciting is just the energy that there is. (00:04:40): Another observation that we've had is engineers who tend to use Codex more open way more PRs. So they're actually opening 70% more PRs than the engineers who aren't using Codex as much. And so might've actually increased since I last looked at the number.
turns.zh:
我现在偶尔还是会写代码。说实话，对于像我这样的管理者来说，使用这些AI工具比手动编码要容易得多了。就我个人和其他工程经理而言，我们在OpenAI的所有代码现在都是由Codex生成的。但更广泛地说，整个团队都充满了活力。内部对这些工具的进展以及Codex带来的好处，大家都倍感振奋。我们很难准确衡量具体有多少代码是由AI生成的，因为绝大多数代码（我敢说接近100%的代码）都是先由AI生成的。不过我们确实能追踪到，目前95%的工程师每天都在使用Codex。（00:04:21）：我们所有的PR（pull request）也都是由Codex每天审核的。基本上，任何合并到生产环境的代码，Codex都会进行审核并提出改进建议。这些都是我们内部观察到的情况，但总体而言，最令人兴奋的是这种活力。
（00:04:40）：我们还发现，那些更频繁使用Codex的工程师提交的PR数量更多。他们的PR数量比不常使用Codex的工程师多70%，而且差距还在不断扩大。我觉得自从我上次查看数据以来，差距可能已经进一步拉大了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay. So just to make sure we hear what you're saying, you're saying all of the code of these 95% engineers at OpenAI is written by AI, it's written and then they review it.
turns.zh: 好的。那我要确保理解你的意思，你是说OpenAI 95%的工程师的所有代码都是由AI生成的，然后再进行审核。

turns.speaker: Sherwin Wu
turns.en: Yep. Yep.
turns.zh: 是的。是的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It's crazy that that's almost not crazy anymore, that we're just getting used to this.
turns.zh: 真难以置信，这已经不再让人觉得不可思议了，我们已经习惯了这种情况。

turns.speaker: Sherwin Wu
turns.en: I think there's still some getting used to, to be clear. There's also, I think, some engineers who I think trust Codex a little bit less, but basically every day I talk to someone who is blown away by something that I can do and their bar of trust or how much they trust the model to do on its own goes up over and over, over time. And there's a quote from Kevin Weil, our VP of science here, and he likes saying, "This is the worst the models will ever be." And so this is the worst that the models will ever be for software engineering as well. And so over time, you just see people trusting it more and more, and then we'll see the models get better and better as well.
turns.zh: 我觉得还是需要一些适应过程。还有，我觉得有些工程师对Codex的信任度稍低一些，但基本上每天我都会和一些人交流，他们对我的工作成果感到惊叹，他们对模型自主完成任务的信任度也越来越高了。凯文·韦尔（Kevin Weil）是我们的科学副总裁，他常说：“模型永远不会完美。” 这句话同样适用于软件工程领域。随着时间推移，你会发现人们越来越信任它，然后模型也会不断优化。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah. Kevin Weil, former podcast guest. He said exactly that line on this podcast a few times.

turns.en: Yeah. Yeah. He's a great user of Codex. I know he's in close touch with the team, gives us great feedback. Not surprised that he uses it. I mean, sorry, it's called OpenClaw now.
turns.zh: 是的。是的。他是Codex的优秀用户。我知道他和团队保持密切联系，提供了很好的反馈。他用这个工具并不奇怪。抱歉，现在它叫OpenClaw了。

turns.en: OpenClaw. Yeah.
turns.zh: 开源软件。是啊。

turns.zh: OpenClaw是个很棒的产品。然后今天早上我看到，嗯，这事儿刚发生不久，但今天早上，我觉得我们也分享过那个MoltBook的案例，看到所有AI智能体在相互交流，感觉真是太不可思议了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It's basically Her is happening in real life is what I'm hearing.
turns.zh: 听说这简直就像《她》在现实生活中上演了一样。

turns.speaker: Sherwin Wu
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 是啊。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So just coming back to this crazy moment we are living through for engineers in particular, we've gone from, you write every line of code to now AI is writing all of your code. I don't know what job has changed more in the past couple years, like job that we didn't expect to change this much where just like the job of an engineer is so different in the entire lifespan of an engineer. In the past couple years, it's now shifted to, "I don't write any more code." How do you imagine the role of an engineer and the job of a software engineer looks in the next couple of years? Just like what is that job?
turns.zh: 回到我们工程师们正在经历的这个疯狂时刻。以前你得亲自写每一行代码，现在AI却能替你写所有代码。我不知道过去几年里还有哪个职业变化如此之大，尤其像工程师这种职业，整个职业生涯都发生了翻天覆地的变化。过去几年里，这个角色已经转变为"我根本不用再写代码了"。未来几年里，你觉得工程师的角色和软件工程师的工作会是什么样子？这个职业究竟会发展成什么样？

turns.speaker: Sherwin Wu
turns.en: Yeah, I mean, it's honestly been really cool to see. And it's part of where the excitement is because the job is likely going to change pretty significantly over the next one to two years. It kind of feels like we're still figuring things out though. And so there's this excitement, I know, especially from some of the software engineers of like, we're in this rare moment, maybe over the next 12 to 24 months where we'll kind of get to figure things out ourselves and set our standards for ourselves. (00:07:52): In terms of where I see this moving, so I think there's the common thing that everyone's saying, which is people are generally... IC engineers are becoming tech leads. They're basically like managers now. They're managing fleets and fleets of agents. I know many of the engineers on my team basically have like 10 to 20 threads kind of being pulled on at the same time. Obviously not active running Codex jobs, but just a lot of parallel threads. They're checking in on what they're doing. They're steering the agents and Codex and giving it feedback. And so their job has kind of really changed from just writing the code itself into being almost like a manager. (00:08:32): In terms of where I think this will go one to two years from now, so one kind of metaphor that I always come back to here is actually is from this programming textbook that I read back in college called SICP. I don't know if you've heard of it, Structure and Interpretation of Computer Programs. So SICP. At MIT, it was really popular and it was actually used as the introductory... It was the textbook for the intro programming course for a very long time. And it kind of has this cult following. It teaches you programming, it teaches you a dialect of Lisp called Scheme. And so it introduces you to functional programs. It's like very mind-opening in that way. (00:09:14): But the thing that was memorable for me about that book, so I kind of read it in college. The very beginning of it kind of describes programming as a discipline and draws this metaphor to basically like sorcery. It says like software engineers are like wizards and programming languages are like incantations and you're like, you're issuing these spells and these spells are kind of like going out and doing things for you. And the challenge is like, what incantation do you have to say to make the program do what you want? (00:09:43): And this book was written in 1980, so this is a while ago. And I think that metaphor has actually kind of persisted over time. And I think it's actually playing out as we move into this new era of vibe coding or just like what software engineering will look like because programming languages were basically using incantations. They've changed over time. And the trend has been that it's been easier and easier to get the computer to do what you want via programming. (00:10:07): And I think the current wave of AI is probably the next stage of that evolution. It is now literally incantations because you can tell Codex, you can tell Cursor exactly what you want to do and then it will go do it for you. And I particularly like the wizard and the sorcery analogy because I think our current state is starting to move towards kind of like The Sorcerer's Apprentice from Fantasia where Mickey Mouse is like, he finds the Sorcerer's hat and he tries to do all these things. (00:10:36): And I just think it's a really apt analogy because one, it's really powerful now. These incantations you can do is extremely high leverage, but you kind of have to know what you're doing. In Sorcerer's Apprentice, the whole plot is like Mickey goes wild, the brooms go crazy and everything's flooding. I think he literally sets the brooms off on a task and then goes to sleep. And so it's like vibe coding at its greatest. And then eventually the old sorcerer comes back and cleans everything up. (00:11:06): And when I see engineers kind of like doing these 20 different Codex threads at a time, there is some skill and there's some seniority and a lot of thought that needs to go into this because you want to make sure that the models aren't going off the rails. You definitely don't want to just completely go away and ignore the thing, but it's also extremely high leverage. A very senior engineer who's really proficient with these tools can now just do way more things via what they're doing. And I think this is also what makes it fun. It literally feels like we're wizards now. It feels like we're closer to making it feel like this magical experience where we're casting all these spells and having software do all these things for you.
turns.zh:
是啊，我是说，这真的很酷，能亲眼见证这一切。这种兴奋感的部分原因在于，未来一到两年内，工作岗位很可能会发生重大变革。不过我觉得我们现在仍在摸索阶段。所以这种兴奋感是真实存在的，我知道，尤其是一些软件工程师，他们觉得自己正处于一个难得的时刻——在接下来的12到24个月里，我们将有机会自主探索并为自己设定标准。  

（00:07:52）：至于我对行业发展的看法，大家都提到IC工程师正逐渐转型为技术主管，他们现在基本上就是管理者了。他们需要管理大量代理团队。我知道我们团队中的许多工程师同时处理着10到20个并行任务。当然不是主动运行Codex任务，而是处理大量并行事务。他们需要检查进度，指导代理和Codex，并提供反馈。因此，他们的工作角色已经从单纯编码转变为类似管理者的角色。  

（00:08:32）：至于未来一到两年的发展方向，我常提到的类比来自我大学时读过的《计算机程序设计艺术》（Structure and Interpretation of Computer Programs，简称SICP）。这本书在麻省理工学院很受欢迎，长期被用作入门级编程课程教材，至今仍有狂热追随者。它不仅教你编程，还教授Lisp语言的Scheme方言，引入函数式编程，思维极具启发性。  

（00:09:14）：但这本书最令我难忘的地方是，我在大学时读到它。开篇将编程描述为一门学科，并将其比作魔法。书中称软件工程师如同巫师，编程语言如同符咒，你下达指令，符咒就会去执行任务。挑战在于，要如何让程序按照你的意愿运行？  

（00:09:43）：这本书写于1980年，已有时日之久。但我认为这种比喻经久不衰。随着我们进入编程即魔法的新时代，这种比喻正在应验。过去编程语言本质上是符咒，如今随着技术进步，计算机执行指令变得越来越容易。  

（00:10:07）：当前的人工智能浪潮或许是这一演进的下一阶段。现在编程简直就是符咒——你可以告诉Codex或Cursor你想要的结果，它们会替你完成任务。我特别喜欢巫师与魔法的比喻，因为我们正朝着《幻想曲》中米奇戴上巫师帽、试图施展魔法的方向发展  

（00:10:36）：我认为这个比喻非常贴切。一方面，这些符咒的威力极强，但你必须得心应手。巫师的学徒阶段正是如此——米奇找到巫师的帽子，却一头扎进未知领域。
学徒，整个剧情就像米奇突然发狂，扫帚乱飞，到处都是洪水。我觉得他就是让扫帚们去执行任务，然后自己去睡觉了。这简直就是最高境界的即兴编程。最后老巫师回来收拾残局。（00:11:06）当我看到工程师们同时处理20个不同的Codex线程时，这需要一定的技巧和资深经验，还得深思熟虑，因为你要确保模型不会失控。你肯定不想完全放任不管，但这同时也带来了极高的生产力。一个精通这些工具的资深工程师，现在能通过现有工作完成更多任务。我觉得这也是乐趣所在。我们现在真的感觉自己像巫师了。这让我们离实现那种神奇的体验更近了一步——我们施展各种魔法，让软件替我们完成所有工作。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I was thinking of The Sorcerer's Apprentice exactly as the metaphor as you were describing that. So I'm glad you went there. A previous podcast guest described it as you have a genie that grants you wishes, and it's a useful frame because you have to be very clear about the wish you want. If you want to be big, how big-
turns.zh: 正如你所描述的，我当时确实把《魔法师的学徒》当作一种隐喻。所以很高兴你提到了这个。之前一位播客嘉宾曾将其比作"你得到一个能满足你愿望的精灵"，这个比喻很贴切，因为你必须清晰地表达自己的愿望。比如，如果你想变得强大，但代价是什么？

turns.speaker: Sherwin Wu
turns.en: Yeah. Or it might be like The Monkey's Paw type thing where it's like you got what you want, but what are the side effects?
turns.zh: 是的。又或者像《猴爪》那种故事，表面上得到了你想要的，但代价是什么？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Right.
turns.zh: 没错。

turns.speaker: Sherwin Wu
turns.en: Yeah. I think that the analogy is great. And yeah, the crazy thing for me is just the staying power of that book, SICP. It's called the wizard book. People call it the wizard book because that is the metaphor that they kind of weave throughout the book. And we've basically reached that point now, which is really cool.
turns.zh: 是啊。我觉得这个比喻很棒。对我来说，最令人惊奇的是《编程之美》这本书的经久不衰。人们称它为"巫师之书"，因为作者在全书中贯穿了这个比喻。而我们现在也到了这个阶段，这真是太棒了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: There's two kind of threads I want to follow here. One is I've been hearing more and more, there's this stress that people feel when their agents aren't working. You fire off all these Codex agents and then you have to stay on top of them, "Oh, shit, one's not working. I'm wasting time." Do you feel that? Do you feel that across your team at all?
turns.zh: 这里有两个我想深入探讨的点。首先，我越来越多地听到人们在代理无法正常工作时感到压力重重。你发送了多个 Codex 代理任务后，却还要时刻关注它们的状态，"天啊，有个代理出问题了，我又得浪费时间了。"你有过这种感受吗？在你的团队中其他人也有这种情况吗？

turns.speaker: Sherwin Wu
turns.en: Yeah, I mean, it happens all the time. And I actually think this is where the interesting part of all of this lies right now because these models aren't perfect, these tools aren't perfect, and we're still trying to figure out how to best interact with Codex or with these AI agents to get work done. We see this come up all the time. There's a particularly interesting team that we have internally. (00:13:05): So there's a team that's actually doing an experiment right now with an OpenAI where they are basically maintaining a 100% Codex written code base. So you'll have the AI write code, but you'll obviously end up rewriting a lot of it and you might need to double-check and change things, but this team is just fully Codex-pilled and just leaning in entirely, and they run into the exact problems that you're describing, which is like, their challenge is, "I want to get this thing, this feature built, but I can't get the agent to do it." (00:13:36): And so usually there's an escape hatch where then you're like, "All right, I'll roll up my sleeves and figure it out." And then instead of using Codex, I might use tab complete and Cursor and things like that. But this team, for the experiment, this team doesn't have that escape hatch. And so then the challenge, how do I get the agent to do this? And I actually think we're going to be publishing a blog post from some of our learnings here, but a lot of fascinating paradigms and best practices are falling out of this. (00:14:03): One interesting thing that we've noticed, and I don't know if this is what you kind of feel, but we definitely feel it here is a lot of the time when the coding agent is not doing what you want, it's usually a problem with context and just like information that you've given it. It's just you've either underspecified or there's just not enough information around how to do something available to the agent, available to Codex. (00:14:25): And so when you have to solve it through that, the challenge is then to add documentation and actually work around this limitation and basically encode more tribal knowledge that's in your head somehow into the code base, either via code comments itself or code structure itself, or via text files like .md files, Skills, any type of additional resources within the repository so that the model can better do its task. (00:14:53): There's a whole bunch of other learnings from this group, which I think is fascinating to explore, but yeah, removing that escape hatch of no longer using the AI has allowed them to start piecing together a lot of the problems that we'll have to solve if we really want to lean into agents.
turns.zh: 是啊，我是说，这种情况经常发生。我觉得这正是当前最有趣的部分，因为这些模型并不完美，这些工具也不完美，我们仍在摸索如何与Codex或这些AI助手进行最佳互动以完成工作。我们经常遇到这种情况。我们内部有一个特别有趣的团队。（00:13:05）：目前有一个团队正在与OpenAI合作进行实验，他们基本上维护着一个完全由Codex编写的代码库。所以你会让AI编写代码，但显然你最终会重写很多代码，可能需要反复检查和修改。但这个团队完全依赖Codex，全力以赴，结果却遇到了你所描述的那些问题，也就是说，他们的挑战在于：“我想要完成这个功能，但却无法让助手做到。” （00:13:36）：通常会有一个退路，比如你会说：“好吧，我会亲自去解决。” 然后就不再使用Codex，而是改用代码补全、光标等工具。但这个团队在实验中没有退路。所以挑战就来了，如何让助手完成这项任务？实际上我们正准备发布一篇博客文章，分享我们的经验教训，但从中也涌现出许多引人入胜的范式和最佳实践。（00:14:03）：我们注意到一个有趣的现象，不知道你是否也有同感，但我们团队深有体会的是，当编码助手无法满足你的需求时，通常是上下文或提供给它的信息存在问题。要么是你的需求描述不清晰，要么是Codex获取信息的渠道不足。（00:14:25）：当你需要自己解决这些问题时，挑战就在于添加文档，克服这些限制，将你脑海中的专业知识以某种方式编码到代码库中，无论是通过代码注释、代码结构，还是通过.md文件、Skills等文本资源，以便模型能更好地完成任务。（00:14:53）：这个团队还有很多其他经验教训，我认为这些都值得深入探讨。但是，取消使用AI的退路，让他们开始逐步解决我们真正想依赖助手时必须面对的诸多难题。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Another issue people run into, you talked about how people are shipping PRs like crazy, a lot more PRs if they're working with AI. Obviously code review is becoming a bigger challenge. Is there anything you've figured out in your team to help speed that up to make that scale and not just create this terrible job for people where they're just sitting there reviewing PRs all day?
turns.zh: 还有一个大家都会遇到的问题，你提到人们疯狂地提交PR（代码提交请求），如果使用AI的话，PR会更多。显然，代码审查正变得越来越困难。你们团队有没有找到什么方法来加快这一过程，让它规模化，而不是让人们整天坐着审核PR，陷入可怕的困境？

turns.speaker: Sherwin Wu
turns.en: Yeah. I mean, one thing is Codex reviews 100% of all of our PRs at this point. And so I actually think, so one really interesting thing that's happened is the things that we tend to hand to the models immediately tend to be the things that annoy us or are the most boring parts of software engineering. It's also why it's more fun now because we get to do more of the fun things. (00:15:50): For me, speaking more for myself, I really hated code reviews. It was like one of the worst things for me. And then I remember in my first job out of college, it was at Quora, I was working on the newsfeed and so I owned the code for the newsfeed. And so I was a reviewer for newsfeed and it was just like the central piece of code that everyone would touch. And so I would just, every morning I'd log in and be like 20 to 30 code reviews. I was just like, oh my goodness, I got to get through all of these. I would procrastinate and then it grows to like 50. And so there's just like a lot of code reviews. (00:16:24): Codex is really good at reviewing code. So actually one thing that we've noticed that 5.2 in particular has gotten extremely strongly adept at is reviewing code and especially when you kind of steer it in the right direction. And so for code reviews, yeah, we create a lot of PRs, but Codex reviews all of them and it makes code reviews go from a, I don't know, 10, 15 minute task to sometimes even just like a two to three minute task because you have a bunch of suggestions already baked in. (00:16:50): A lot of the times people will, especially for small PRs, you actually don't even need people to review. We kind of trust Codex in this way. The original author kind of looks at Codex. The benefit of code reviews to have a second pair of eyes to make sure that you're not doing anything dumb. Codex is a pretty smart second pair of eyes at this point. And so that's something that we've heavily leaned into. (00:17:10): The general CI process and the post kind of push and deployment process has also been heavily automated via Codex internally at this point. If you talk to a lot of engineers, the thing that annoys them the most is after you've written your beautiful code, how do you get it into production? You got to run through all these tests, you got to lint errors, code review. There's a lot of automated stuff you can do with Codex. And so we've actually built some tools internally that help automate that process, automate the lint. If there's like a lint error, it's a very easy Codex fix and it could just patch it and then kind of restart the CI process. So all of that is, we're trying to collapse into as little work for an engineer as possible, and the byproduct of which is they can now merge and push out a lot more PRs.
turns.zh: 是的。我的意思是，目前Codex会对我们所有拉取请求（PR）进行100%代码审查。所以我觉得一个很有趣的现象是，我们倾向于立即把一些任务交给模型处理的，往往都是那些最让我们头疼、最枯燥的软件工程部分。这也是现在更有趣的原因——因为我们能做更多有趣的工作了。（00:15:50）：就我个人而言，我以前特别讨厌代码审查。这简直是我最头疼的事之一。我记得大学毕业后的第一份工作是在Quora，当时我在做新闻推送功能，负责该功能的代码。作为新闻推送的代码审查者，那段代码是每个人都会接触的核心部分。所以每天早上登录后，就能看到20到30个代码审查任务。我当时就想，天哪，这些任务得赶紧处理完。结果一拖再拖，最后积压到50个。总之，代码审查任务实在太多了。（00:16:24）：Codex在代码审查方面确实很出色。特别是5.2版本，我们发现它在这方面变得极其高效，尤其是当你给它正确的指导方向时。就代码审查而言，我们确实会创建很多PR，但Codex会全部审查一遍。这让代码审查从原本需要10到15分钟的任务，缩短到只需两到三分钟，因为很多建议都已经内置了。（00:16:50）：很多时候，尤其是对于小型PR，你甚至不需要人工审查。我们现在就这样信任Codex。代码审查的意义在于多一双眼睛，确保你没有做任何愚蠢的事情。就目前而言，Codex就是一双相当聪明的眼睛。所以这方面我们投入了大量精力。（00:17:10）：整个持续集成（CI）流程和后续的推送及部署流程，现在在内部也已经通过Codex实现了高度自动化。如果你和很多工程师交流，他们最头疼的是写出漂亮代码后，如何让它上线？你得跑一遍测试，检查代码是否有lint错误，再进行代码审查。用Codex可以自动化很多这些步骤。我们内部开发了一些工具来自动化这些流程，比如lint检查。若有lint错误，Codex可以轻松修复，然后重新启动CI流程。总之，我们正努力把工程师的工作量压缩到最小，而其副产品就是他们现在能合并和推送更多的PR了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Codex writing the code, Codex reviewing its own code. I'm curious if you are open to using other models to review your model's work. Is that a path or is it just, it's good enough, we don't need anything else.
turns.zh: Codex写代码，Codex审查自己的代码。我很好奇，你们是否愿意使用其他模型来审查你们模型的工作。有没有可能走这条路，还是说现有方案已经足够好了？

turns.speaker: Sherwin Wu
turns.en: So I will say there's definitely a circular thing here. And going back to Sorcerer's Apprentice, you want to make sure you're not letting the brooms go crazy here. And so we're very thoughtful, I'd say, around which PRs are completely just Codex-reviewed. Most people still obviously take a look at their PRs. And so it's not like it's going to zero. It's more like going from 100% attention to 30% attention, which just helps things push through. (00:18:30): In terms of multiple models, so we obviously test a lot of models internally, and so we have a lot of those. We use external models less. We think it's important to dog food our own models and get feedback there, but you can also, there are a lot of internal variants of models that you can use to give you a different perspectives here as well, and we found that to work quite well.
turns.zh: 好的，我要说这里肯定存在一个循环的问题。回到《魔法师的学徒》这个例子，你要确保不让扫帚在这里失控。说实话，我们对哪些 PR 完全由 Codex 审核非常谨慎。显然，大多数人还是会亲自审阅他们的 PR。所以这并不是说完全不审核，而是从 100% 关注降到 30% 关注，这样能更高效地推进工作进度。 （00:18:30）：关于多模型的问题，我们内部确实测试了很多模型，但外部模型的使用相对较少。我们认为用自己的模型进行迭代并获取反馈很重要，但你也可以利用模型的内部变体来获得不同的视角，我们发现这种方法效果不错。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay. So just to make sure we get a barometer of today's world at OpenAI in terms of AI and code, just so I understand, and then I want to move on to different topic. 100% of code across OpenAI is written by Codex at this point. Is that the way to frame it?
turns.zh: 好的。为了更好地了解 OpenAI 在 AI 和代码方面的现状，我需要确认一下，100% OpenAI 的代码都是由 Codex 编写的吗？是这样理解吗？

turns.speaker: Sherwin Wu
turns.en: I wouldn't make the statement that 100% of code running in production today is written by AI. And it's kind of hard to do attribution there, but almost every engineer heavily uses Codex in all of their tasks at this point. And so if I were to guesstimate, just the vast majority of code at this point was probably authored by AI.
turns.zh: 我不会说现在生产环境中 100% 的代码都是由 AI 编写的。这部分很难追溯到具体来源，但几乎每个工程师现在在所有任务中都大量使用 Codex。如果要猜测的话，目前绝大多数代码很可能是由 AI 编写的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Incredible. Okay. So there's a lot of talk, and we've been talking about the IC role, the work of an IC engineer. There's less talk about the changing role of a manager, especially an engineering manager. How has your life as a manager changed with the rise of AI? And just where do you think managers, what's the role of a manager in the future?
turns.zh: 太不可思议了。好的。我们一直在讨论 IC 工程师的角色，但对工程经理角色变化的讨论较少。随着 AI 兴起，您作为经理的生活发生了哪些变化？您认为未来经理的角色会是什么？

turns.speaker: Sherwin Wu
turns.en: It's definitely changed less than an engineer. There's no Codex for managers just yet. However, I use Codex quite a bit for some of the more managery tasks that I do. I'd say a couple things are changing. There are like some trends. So I don't think it's changed that much yet, but I see trends, and I think if you play it out, you can see where a lot of this is going. One thing that's becoming increasingly clear is Codex really empowers top performers to be a lot more productive. And I think this is maybe true for AI more broadly across society, which is the people who really lean in or the people who have high agency or will really get good at these tools, will kind of supercharge themselves. And so I'm kind of noticing this now as well, which is like the top performers kind of end up being a lot more productive. And so you see a broader spread in team productivity in this way. (00:20:50): So one thing that I've always done as a management philosophy is to spend actually the majority of my time with top performers, just like make sure they're unblocked, make sure they're happy, make sure they feel productive and they feel heard. I think this is even more true in an AI world where your top performers are going to just really be shooting ahead using these tools. I think one example is the team that's maintaining a 100% Codex generated code base, just letting them rip and see what's happening there. It is something that's paid dividends. (00:21:20): So I think that's kind of one trend that I'm seeing where spending even more time with top performers for managers I think is likely going to continue. The other thing is, so this is more an observation, but my sense is with a lot of these AI tools available to managers, so less like writing code, but just things like ChatGPT with organizational knowledge, like being able to do research and understanding organizational context a lot better. (00:21:50): Another good example is we're doing performance reviews right now and it's actually really easy to use ChatGPT with internal knowledge hooked up to GitHub and our Notion Docs and Google Docs to get a really good sense of what this person has done over the last 12 months and writing a little deep research report for it. My sense is I think managers will be able to manage much larger teams in this world, kind of like how software engineers are managing 20 to 30 Codexes. My sense of these tools will allow managers, people managers to be higher leveraged and it will allow them to manage teams of way more than the current best practice of, I think it's like six to eight for software engineering. (00:22:30): You kind of see this applied to the non-engineering domains like support or operations where previously the size of a support team might be limited, but as you can pass off more things to agents, you can actually do more work and also manage more people this way. (00:22:50): I think the same thing might happen for people management as well, especially in tech companies. And we're already seeing this. There's some teams where there are EMs managing quite a few people and they're doing it pretty adeptly because of some of these tools where they can get higher leverage and understand what their team's doing, understand organizational context a little bit better and operate in that way.
turns.zh: 相较于工程师，管理者的变化确实较小。目前还没有针对管理者的官方指南。不过，我确实会频繁使用Codex来处理一些管理任务。我认为有几个方面正在发生变化。可以看到一些趋势。虽然目前变化不算显著，但我能预见到未来的发展方向。越来越明显的是，Codex确实能助力顶尖人才提高工作效率。我认为这在整个社会层面也适用于AI领域——那些积极主动、能高效运用工具的人会自我提升。我最近也注意到，顶尖人才的工作效率确实显著提高，因此团队整体生产力也随之提升。（00:20:50）作为管理理念，我一直致力于将大部分时间投入到顶尖人才身上，确保他们能顺利开展工作，保持愉悦感和成就感。在AI时代，这一点尤为重要，因为顶尖人才会借助这些工具实现飞跃式进步。比如，有个团队完全使用Codex生成的代码库，他们可以自由发挥，观察其效果，这种做法成效显著。（00:21:20）我认为管理者与顶尖人才深度互动的趋势将持续下去。另一个观察是，AI工具为管理者提供了更多可能性，比如利用ChatGPT结合内部知识库，进行组织研究和情境理解。这类工具能让管理者更高效地管理团队，效益远超当前软件工程师管理20到30个Codex的标准。（00:22:30）这类工具还适用于非技术领域，如客服或运维。过去客服团队规模受限，但借助智能助手可以处理更多事务，从而提升工作效率和管理能力。（00:22:50）同样的趋势或将延续至人力管理领域，尤其是在科技公司。我们已经看到一些例子：人力资源经理借助工具管理多个团队，效率显著提升。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love this advice that the way you described it is you've always leaned into top performers and spent more time with them, unblocked them, make sure they're happy. The way Marc Andreessen was just on the podcast, the way he phrased it is AI makes good people better and it makes great people exceptional. And what you're saying here is just doing this more and more is probably the right move, spending more time with the best people on your team to unblock them, make sure they have everything they need.
turns.zh: 我很喜欢你提到的这个建议——正如你所描述的，你一直倾向于培养表现出色的员工，花更多时间与他们交流，帮助他们突破瓶颈，确保他们快乐工作。马克·安德森（Marc Andreessen）在播客中的说法也很有道理：人工智能能让优秀的人更出色，让卓越的人更加非凡。而你在这里提到的做法——不断加强这些努力，花更多时间与团队中的顶尖人才沟通，帮助他们突破障碍，确保他们获得所需支持——很可能是正确的方向。

turns.speaker: Sherwin Wu
turns.en: Yeah. A very good example right now is there are, I would say, a group of engineers internally who are really Codex-pilled and are thinking through what the best practices are for interacting with this model. And that is just an extremely high leverage thing for them to do. And so just like as a manager, I'm just like, yeah, go explore this. Whatever best practices come out of this, we have to share with the org. We do all these knowledge sharing sessions, we'll share documents and best practices everywhere. So things like that just elevate everyone. And so I view that as another example of this trend that we're seeing where the top performers really get exceptional.
turns.zh: 是的。目前有一个很好的例子，我可以说，公司内部有一群工程师，他们对Codex（一个深度学习框架）非常精通，正在深入思考与该模型交互的最佳实践。这对他们来说是极具价值的工作。作为管理者，我会鼓励他们去探索。无论得出什么最佳实践，我们都必须与整个团队分享。我们会定期举办知识分享会，广泛传播相关文档和最佳实践。这样的举措能让每个人都受益。我认为这再次印证了我们所观察到的趋势——表现卓越的员工确实能脱颖而出。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: People just have a sense, this is big. AI is changing so much. The world is changing. It's going to be a huge deal. What do you think people aren't pricing in yet into what will change and to where things are heading? Just like what's an example of something you think are like, okay, we're not realizing this yet.
turns.zh: 人们普遍感觉到，人工智能的影响深远。世界正在发生巨变，这将带来翻天覆地的变化。你认为人们目前还未充分预见哪些变化，或者未能意识到事态的走向？能否举个例子，说明哪些领域的潜力尚未被充分认识？

turns.speaker: Sherwin Wu
turns.en: So one of my favorite kind of phrases or things that have come out of this whole AI wave is the idea of the one person billion dollar startup. I actually think Sam may have keyed it or Sam may have been the first one to say it, but it's fascinating to think about. It's like, yeah, if people are so high leveraged, at some point there will likely be a one person billion dollar startup. (00:24:53): And while I think that's really, really cool, I think people aren't really pricing the second or third order effects of this. And really, because what the one person billion dollar startup implies is that one person can just have so much more agency and so much more leverage using one of these tools that it is just super easy for them to get everything done that they need to for their business to ultimately create something that's a billion dollars. (00:25:19): But I think there are a couple other implications of this. So one of them is if it's easy for a person to create a one person... or if it's possible for a person to create a one person billion dollar startup, it also means it's way easier for people to just create startups in general. I actually think this will... One second order effect of this is I think there's just going to be a huge startup boom and small SMB style boom where anyone can build software for anything. (00:25:45): One, you're kind of starting to see this play out in the AI startup scene where software's became a lot more vertical oriented, where these verticals, like creating some AI tool for some vertical tends to work quite well because you really lean into that particular domain, you really understand the use case for it. And so if you play out AI, there's no reason why you can't have like 100x more of these startups. (00:26:13): And so I think one world that we might end up seeing happen is in order to enable a one person billion dollar startup, there might be like a hundred other small startups building bespoke software that works extremely well to support other types of small one person billion dollar startups. And so I think we might actually enter into a golden age of like B2B SaaS and just like software and startups in general. (00:26:38): And so I think that's a really interesting trend to kind of see because as it gets easier and easier to build software, as it's easier and easier to run a company, you might actually just end up seeing way more of these startups. And so the way I've been thinking about is like, yeah, there might be one one person billion dollar startup, but there might be like 100 $100 million startups. There might be tens of thousands of $10 million startups. And as an individual, it's actually pretty great to have a $10 million business. That's like enough for... You're set for life at that point. And so we might really see an explosion in that way. And I feel like people aren't really pressing that in. (00:27:20): There's another kind of third order effect of this. And again, all of these, as you get to the further and further out predictions, I think there's a lot of uncertainty. I think if we end up moving to this world where you end up with these kind of micro companies building software that works for one or two people who own the company and are working there, I think the startup ecosystem will change. I think the VC ecosystem will change. We might end up in a world where there's just like a handful of big players that are offering platforms and supporting all of these startups, but the types of venture scale return startups that can really 100 or 1,000x your investment might actually end up shrinking if you end up having a bunch of these smaller 10 to 50 million dollar companies, which are not great for venture startup returns, but are great for the individuals, the high agency individuals who are now really leaning into AI to build these businesses for themselves.
turns.zh:
让我来分享一下我最喜欢的AI浪潮带来的一个现象——"一人亿万美元创业公司"。实际上，我觉得山姆（Sam Altman）可能最先提出了这个概念，或者他是第一个说出这个想法的人。但仔细想想，这真的很吸引人。是的，如果人们的杠杆效应足够高，最终很可能就会出现一人亿万美元的创业公司。（00:24:53）虽然我觉得这真的很酷，但我认为人们并没有真正意识到其二阶和三阶效应。毕竟，一人亿万美元创业公司意味着一个人可以利用这些工具获得更大的自主权和更高的杠杆效应，从而轻松完成业务所需的一切，最终创造出价值十亿美元的企业。（00:25:19）但我认为还有其他影响。首先，如果一个人能轻松创办一家亿万美元的创业公司，这意味着人们创办初创公司的门槛会大大降低。我认为这将引发一场创业热潮，尤其是中小型企业的发展热潮，任何人都能为任何领域开发软件。（00:25:45）目前，我们已经在AI创业领域看到这种趋势——软件变得更加垂直化。针对特定垂直领域开发AI工具往往效果显著，因为你能深入该领域，真正理解其应用场景。若延伸到AI领域，完全可以想象会有100倍于现在的此类创业公司。（00:26:13）我认为未来可能出现的场景是，为了支持一人亿万美元的创业公司，会有数百家小型初创公司开发定制软件，而这些软件将极大地支持其他小型一人亿万美元创业公司。因此，我们可能会迎来B2B SaaS和初创公司的黄金时代。（00:26:38）这确实是一个很有趣的趋势，因为开发软件和运营公司变得越来越容易，创业公司数量可能会激增。我认为人们对此关注不足。（00:27:20）还有第三阶效应。当然，越是长远的预测，就越不确定。我认为如果我们真的进入这样一个世界——微型公司为一到两名所有者和员工开发软件——创业生态系统将发生变化，风险投资生态系统也将改变。可能最终只剩下少数大玩家提供平台支持所有这些初创公司，但那些能让投资回报增长100或1000倍的风险投资级回报型初创公司可能会消失。
实际上，如果你最终拥有大量规模较小的1000万至5000万美元的公司，市场规模最终可能会缩小。这对风险投资回报来说并非利好，但对个人而言却是个好消息，尤其是那些精英创业者，他们如今正积极投身人工智能领域，为自己打造商业帝国。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love how many order effects we've been through. I want to hear the fourth order effect now, Sherwin. I'm just joking.
turns.zh: 我很喜欢我们探讨过的多个订单效应。现在我想听听第四阶订单效应，谢尔文。我只是开玩笑的。

turns.speaker: Sherwin Wu
turns.en: Fourth order is too giga-brain for me. I can't think that far ahead.
turns.zh: 第四阶订单效应对我来说太烧脑了。我根本想不到那么远的未来。

turns.en: It's like inception where just everything gets slower every time you go deeper into selling every layer. Okay. So the billion dollar startup, I think about this a lot because I'm not going to be a billion dollar startup because what I'm doing is not venture scale in any way and not super high leveraged, but just seeing how many support tickets I get from just the most ridiculous things, it's hard for me to imagine one person... Like I'm bearish on this billion dollar startup. I just want to share this thought simply because of the support costs. Even if AI is helping you at a billion dollars, just like unless your ACVs are very high and you have very few customers, just dealing with support. And people are like, they can solve their own problems, but they're like, "Eh, I'll email support, ask about this thing." (00:29:12): Just dealing with that is hard to scale is in my experience. So in my opinion, unless you have a bunch of contractors, which I don't know, does that count as a single person company, I feel like it's very difficult to scale a billion dollar startup and not have someone helping you with at least the support work. And AI I think will only take you so far.
turns.zh: 这就像《盗梦空间》里，每次深入到销售的每一层，事情就变得越慢。好吧。所以关于十亿美元级初创公司，我经常思考这个问题，因为我自己永远做不到十亿美元级初创公司——我现在做的事情根本不具备风险投资规模，也没有超高杠杆。但光是处理用户提出的那些最奇葩的支持请求，就让我难以想象一个人能应付得来。比如我对十亿美元级初创公司持悲观态度。单纯是因为支持成本的问题。即使人工智能能帮你处理十亿美元级的业务，但除非你的客户终身价值非常高且客户数量极少，否则光是处理支持请求就够头疼了。人们会说“自己能解决问题”，但最后还是发邮件问客服。（00:29:12）在我的经验里，光是处理支持请求就很难实现规模化。所以在我看来，除非你有一群承包商（虽然我不确定这算不算单人公司），要不然十亿美元级初创公司很难不至少有专人负责支持工作。况且我觉得人工智能能发挥的作用也是有限的。

turns.speaker: Sherwin Wu
turns.en: So I think that's true. And actually, I think my view on it is slightly different, which is I think that Lenny's Podcast might end up becoming a billion dollar startup, but what I think might happen is instead of you kind of being the one person who has to dispatch an AI to solve and fix those support tickets, I think what might end up happening is there might be a whole smattering of other startups that are building software and super tailored towards what you might need. And so there might be 10 or 20 startups that build support software for podcasts and newsletters. And that might be a one person startup. It doesn't need to be a big one. And they might be able to just code up this product very, very easily. They're able to build their own thing. And because it's so tailored and unique and hopefully useful for you, it might be something that you purchase as the one person billion dollar startup.
turns.zh: 所以我觉得这说得对。实际上，我对此的看法略有不同。我认为《Lenny's Podcast》最终可能会成为十亿美元级初创公司，但可能的情况是，你不必亲自派人工智能去处理那些支持请求，而是会有大量其他初创公司为你量身定制软件。可能会出现10到20家为播客和新闻通讯提供支持软件的初创公司。这些公司可能都是单人公司，不必规模庞大。他们能很轻松地开发出这类产品。因为产品高度定制化、独一无二且希望对用户有用，你可能会把它当作十亿美元级初创公司的配套产品购买。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I would buy that. I would buy that.
turns.zh: 我愿意买单。我愿意买单。

turns.speaker: Sherwin Wu
turns.en: Yeah. There's a question of what you in-house and what you outsource. And what I think might happen is because the cost of running software and building products is collapsing so much, you might end up outsourcing a lot of this. And in doing so, reducing the size of your company. And so that's kind of the world that I think might end up happening. Again, there's high certainty in what might play out here, but the end result still might be one person driving this high massive leveraged company that might actually reach a billion dollars.
turns.zh: 是的。关键在于内部处理和外包服务的平衡。我认为随着软件开发和产品构建成本急剧下降，越来越多的工作会被外包出去，从而缩小公司规模。这可能就是未来会发生的情况。当然，具体发展路径存在高度不确定性，但最终结果很可能是由一个人掌控这家高杠杆率的公司，最终真正达到十亿美元规模。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I could see that. I also think about Peter at Clawdbot/Moltbot/OpenClaw of just how barraged he is right now by all these asks and emails and pings and DMs and PRs, just like, I'm curious to... And he's not even making any money off this thing.
turns.zh: 我能理解这种情况。我也想到Peter在Clawdbot/Moltbot/OpenClaw上被各种提问、邮件、通知、私信和公关请求淹没的情景。真想知道……而且他甚至还没从这项业务中赚到钱。

turns.speaker: Sherwin Wu
turns.en: Yeah, I can't imagine what it's like to be him right now. It must be absolutely insane. It's probably like the months after we launched ChatGPT, the craziness that was.

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: As one man. He's coming out on the pod, by the way, in a week.

turns.speaker: Sherwin Wu
turns.en: Oh, that's exciting. Yeah.
turns.zh: 哦，太令人兴奋了。是啊。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Maybe the fourth order effect is distribution becomes increasingly important because there are so many freaking things trying to get your attention. So people with an audience and platform I think become more and more valuable, which is good stuff. (00:31:40): Okay. I wanted to come back actually to your management stuff. So I really loved your insight about spending more time with top performers has been really successful to you. Just thinking about you as a manager of a team that is building the platform that powers basically the entire AI economy, like every AI startup is building on your API. Clearly you're doing a great job. What other kind of core management lessons have you learned? What do you find is really important and key to your success as a manager of engineers and just people?
turns.zh: 或许第四阶效应是，随着越来越多疯狂的信息争夺你的注意力，分发渠道的重要性会日益凸显。因此，我认为拥有受众和平台的人会变得越来越有价值，这确实是个好现象。（00:31:40）：好的。其实我还想再聊聊你的管理心得。关于多花时间与顶尖员工沟通的见解，对你来说确实很有效。想想你作为一个团队的管理者，这个团队正在构建一个支撑整个AI经济的基础平台——几乎每家AI初创公司都在使用你们的API。显然你做得很棒。作为工程师和团队的管理者，你还学到了哪些核心管理经验？哪些方面对你的成功至关重要？

turns.speaker: Sherwin Wu
turns.en: Yeah. I think a lot of the lessons that I've learned here, I don't know how specific it is to the OpenAI API or some of our enterprise products in particular. I think my management philosophy has obviously changed over time, but I think it's probably stayed the same more than it's changed over time. (00:32:31): One of these principles is what I talked to you about before, which is spending a lot of time with top performers, like actually spending... And to be very concrete, it's like more than 50% of your time with your top performers, with maybe your top 10% performers, and really, really trying your best to empower them. (00:32:48): The way that I think about it is kind of come back to this analogy of software engineer as a surgeon, which comes from The Mythical Man-Month. So actually, it's funny. So I pull it from the book, but in the book, they actually described this world where I think they were predicting the future because I think the book was written in the '70s or something. (00:33:10): They said that software engineering might end up moving into a world where that software engineers are like surgeons or in a surgery room, there's one person doing the work and there's the one person cutting or whatever and doing all the surgery, and everyone else in the room is there to just support them. It's like the nurse and the assistant and the resident and the fellow and then the surgeon's like, "I need a scalpel," and they give them scalpel and then they're like, "I need this tool and this machine," and they'll bring it over." Everyone's there to just support the one surgeon. A. (00:33:40): Nd so The Mythical Man-Month actually predicted that that is kind of the direction that software engineering's going to go. I don't think that's exactly played out where it's much more collaborative and it's not only one person doing the work, but I've always really liked that analogy. And that analogy is actually what I strive to emulate in my own management philosophy, which is software engineering isn't really like surgery where it's not just one person doing the work, but the way in which I like treating the people on my team and the way that I act as a manager is I want to empower them, make them feel like they're a surgeon. And insofar as making sure that I'm supporting them and making sure they have everything that they need to do their work, and it feels like they have an army of people kind of supporting them and looking around corners and giving them everything that they need when it's really just me as the manager. (00:34:27): And so the example that I give is looking around corners and unblocking people, especially from an organizational perspective, is extremely, extremely useful. And again, going back to the AI conversations, even more important nowadays, right? If people are just cranking PR after PR, the main thing bottlenecking progress and shipping something tends to be organizational or process oriented. And if you as a manager can look around corners and kind of unblock the team, if the surgeon needs a scalpel, but the manager already has a scalpel ready for them, that's the best case scenario. That's kind of the way that I approach management and especially engineering management. And so that's something that's really, really stuck with me over time. And even though software engineers aren't exactly surgeons, that metaphor has always stayed in my mind as I've progressed in my career.
turns.zh: 是的。我觉得我在这里学到的很多经验教训，并不局限于OpenAI API或我们某些企业产品。我认为我的管理理念显然是随着时间而变化的，但与其说它随时间而改变，不如说它在很大程度上保持了原样。（00:32:31）：其中一条原则是我之前跟你谈过的，那就是花大量时间与表现出色的人在一起。比如，实际上你要把50%以上的时间花在顶尖员工身上，可能甚至是前10%的表现优异者身上，并且尽最大努力赋予他们权力。（00:32:48）：我对此的理解可以追溯到《神话般的人月》一书中提到的软件工程师如同外科医生的比喻。说起来挺有趣的，我从书中借鉴了这个比喻，但在书中，他们实际上描绘了一个未来世界——我认为这本书写于70年代左右。（00:33:10）：他们说，软件工程可能会发展成一个外科医生式的环境，即一名程序员在手术室里进行编码，周围有护士、助手、实习医生等人员提供支持。就像外科医生需要手术刀，助手会立即递给他，然后他又需要其他工具，助手也会及时提供。这就是外科医生和团队成员的典型互动模式。我努力效仿这种管理理念，认为软件工程不应像外科手术那样由单人主导，而是要赋予团队成员权力，帮助他们像外科医生一样自主工作。（00:34:27）：比如，我提到的"未雨绸缪"和"为团队排除障碍"等技巧，在组织层面尤为重要。如今在AI项目中，如果团队成员只能机械地完成PR任务，阻碍进展和交付的主要原因往往是组织或流程层面的障碍。作为管理者，如果能未雨绸缪地为团队排除障碍，就像外科医生需要手术刀而助手已提前准备好一样，这才是理想的管理境界。这就是我管理理念的核心，尤其是在工程管理方面。虽然软件工程师并非真正的外科医生，但这个比喻始终深深印在我的职业生涯记忆中。

turns.en: We just had an insight right here.

(00:44:58): And this phrase that I thought was really good, which is the models will eat your scaffolding for breakfast. If you rewind back to 2022, right when ChatGPT launched, these models are pretty raw and there was like all this product scaffolding and things, especially in the developer space, to basically try and steer the model and build a scaffolding around it to get it to do what you want. Like agent frameworks, there's like vector stores I think was like really popular back then and just like a whole smattering of tools here. (00:45:30): And as you've kind of seen the field play out, the models have just changed so much and gotten so much better that they ended up literally eating some of the scaffolding. I could see a world where at some point that's no longer useful, where the model can actually manage all that themselves, or there might be, it's hard to predict, but might move on to some new paradigm where you'll already need this file-based Skills type thing. (00:46:05): You have literally seen this play out where like the agent frameworks I think are a little less useful now. There was a period of time in like 2023 where we thought vector stores is going to be like the main way for you to bring organizational context into the models and you need to vectorize and embed every bit of your corpuses and then you need to do all this work to figure out the vector search to optimize that to fill out the right information at the right time. (00:46:29): All of that is scaffolding because the model was not good enough. And turns out, in this case, it turns out as the models get better, a better approach is actually to take out a lot of that logic and trust the model and give it a set of tools for search. It doesn't need to be a vector store. You could actually just hook it up to any type of search. It could literally be files on a file system like Skills and AGENTS.md to kind of steer it as well. Obviously there's still a place for vector stores. I know a lot of companies still using it, but the entire scaffolding around that and building an entire ecosystem around that and assuming that's the only scaffolding that you need has really changed. (00:47:05): And so tying this back to the like, you don't always have to listen to your customers. Because the field is changing so much at any point in time, a lot of people are kind of in this local maximum. And if you just blindly listen to your customers, they'll be like, "Yeah, I want a better vector store. I want a better agent framework for this." And if you had just kind of only chased down that path, it actually would've led you to build something that again is the local maxima. (00:47:31): Whereas as the models get better, we've had to reinvent and kind of rethink the right abstractions and the right tools and frameworks to build around these models. I think that's what makes it exciting, but it also means when you talk to customers, you kind of need to balance the exact feedback that they want with where you think the models are going and where you think things will trend over the next one to two years.

我不确定这观点是否有那么大的说服力。我认为关键在于，你显然应该和客户沟通。但就AI领域而言，尤其是过去三年我参与API开发并见证其快速演进的经历，模型本身及其相关技术正以极快的速度迭代，往往会自我颠覆——尤其是在工具和框架层面。本周早些时候，我读到一篇X平台文章，作者是Nicolas，他是Fintool初创公司的创始人。在文中，他分享了在金融服务领域构建AI智能体时积累的最佳实践。

（00:44:58）：文中有一句话让我深有共鸣——“模型会把你的框架当早餐吃掉”。回溯到2022年，ChatGPT刚推出时，那些模型还很粗糙，开发者们急于用各种产品框架来引导模型，围绕模型搭建框架以实现预期功能。比如智能体框架、向量存储等，当时这些工具风靡一时。（00:45:30）：但随着模型性能的飞跃，许多框架已被淘汰。Nicolas提到的当前流行框架是基于Skills的文件式上下文管理。我能预见到未来某个时刻，这类框架可能不再适用，模型将自主管理所有上下文。（00:46:05）：智能体框架的衰落已成事实。2023年曾有人认为向量存储是引入组织上下文的关键，但实践证明，随着模型性能提升，采用向量搜索的逻辑已被简化为搜索引擎接口，无需复杂的向量存储。（00:46:29）：这些框架本质上是权宜之计，因为模型尚未达到理想状态。随着模型进步，自然会转向信任模型并为其提供搜索工具，无需依赖向量存储。（00:47:05）：回到核心观点：不必总是听从客户意见。领域发展迅速，许多人会陷入局部最优陷阱。如果盲目追随客户需求，最终只能构建出不合时宜的方案。
再次强调，这是局部最大值。（00:47:31）：随着模型性能的提升，我们不得不重新发明并重新思考合适的抽象概念、工具和框架来构建这些模型。令人兴奋但又有些头疼的是，这是一个不断变化的目标。因此，当前零星分布的工具和框架很可能需要随着模型变得更智能、更出色而进行重大升级和调整。但这正是这个领域开发的本质。我认为这正是它令人兴奋之处，但同时也意味着，当你与客户沟通时，你需要在他们期望的具体反馈与你对模型发展方向的判断，以及未来一到两年技术趋势的预测之间找到平衡。
