turns.speaker: Sherwin Wu
turns.en: My general advice, and I've been giving this to people for a while and I think it's still true today is make sure you're building for where the models are going and not where they are today. It's clearly a moving target. And I think a lot of the companies that I've seen, startups that I've seen really, really do well is they build a product for an ideal type of capability that is like maybe 80% of the way there today. And they end up having a product that kind of works, but is just almost there. (00:49:39): But then as the models get better, suddenly it might click and then their product now is incredible because it works like maybe with like o3, at some point it suddenly works with 5.1, 5.2, suddenly it unlocks it, but they're building these products with the model capability improvements in mind. And with that, you end up creating an experience that's way better than if you had assumed that it's static in the first place. (00:50:02): And so that'd be my general advice, which is build for where the models are going and not where they are today. You end up building a better product. You may need to wait a little bit, but the models are getting so much better so quickly, you often don't need to wait that long.
turns.zh: 我的总体建议是——我已经向很多人分享过这个观点，至今依然适用：要确保你的开发方向紧跟模型的发展趋势，而非停留在当前阶段。这显然是一个不断变化的目标。许多我见过的成功初创公司，都会为理想的能力类型打造产品，比如当前可能只达成80%的目标。但最终产品能基本运行，虽然还有改进空间。（00:49:39）但随着模型不断进步，某个功能可能突然触发——比如最初支持o3版本，后来升级到5.1和5.2版本，功能就解锁了。而这些产品正是基于模型能力的迭代而打造的。（00:50:02）所以我的建议是：要为模型的发展方向而非当前状态进行开发。这样你才能打造出更优质的产品。当然可能需要等待一段时间，但模型进步如此之快，等待时间往往没那么长。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So to follow that thread, like in the next 6 to 12 months, where is the API heading? Where's the platform heading? Where are the models heading? As much as you can share, I know there's a lot of secrets here, that maybe you're most excited about, or you think that people should start to prepare for and however much you can share?
turns.zh: 那么接下来的6到12个月，API会走向何方？平台会如何发展？模型又将去向何处？如果方便的话，能否透露一些信息？我知道这里有很多保密内容，但有没有你最为期待的进展，或者你认为人们应该提前准备的方向？

turns.speaker: Sherwin Wu
turns.en: I mean, so the obvious one is how long of a task these models can do coherently. So there's like the METR benchmark that I think tracks software engineering tasks and how long of a task can these models do 50% of the time, 80% of the time. I think we're at something like multi-hour tasks being able to be done by... software engineering tasks being able to be done by these frontier models 50% of the time. And then I think 80% is something like just under an hour. (00:51:06): But the sobering thing about that chart is they plot all the previous models on this chart as well. So you can really see the trend of this. That's something that I'm really excited about, which is, I actually think products today really optimize for tasks that the model can do for minutes at a time. Even Codex and the coding tools, I'd say, it's in the CLI, you're kind of seeing it be interactive. (00:51:28): It's really quite optimized well for maybe at most 10 minute type tasks. I have seen people push Codex to the limit and do multi-hour long tasks. But again, I think that's more of the exception. But if you follow this trend, I think in the next 12, 18 months, we could see models that could do multi-hour long tests very, very coherently. At some point it might reach like six hours, a day long task where you kind of like dispatch it and have it do things on its own for a while. The types of products you build around that will look very different. You want to give the model feedback. You obviously don't want it to completely run wild for a day. Maybe you do, but you probably don't. And then the universe of things you can have the model do really expand. So that's something that I'm really, really excited about seeing. (00:52:15): Another thing over the next 12 to 18 months, what I think would be really cool is improvements in the multimodal models. And actually by multimodality, I'm mostly thinking about audio here where the models are pretty good at audio, I think they're going to get a lot better at audio over the next 6 to 12 months, especially the native multimodal models, the speech to speech ones. I think there's also interesting work being done around new types of models and architectures on the multimodal audio side as well. (00:52:48): But audio, especially in the enterprise and in a business setting, I think is a hugely underrated domain still. Everyone talks about coding, it's all text, but we're talking in audio. A lot of the world's business is done via audio. A lot of services and operations are done via talking and audio. And so I think that area is going to look very exciting in the next 12, 18 months. And I think there will be even more unlock for what we can do with audio models there as well.
turns.zh: 我的意思是，这些模型能够连贯地处理多长时间的任务？比如，METR基准测试就追踪了软件工程任务，以及这些模型在50%或80%的时间内能够处理多长时间的任务。我认为目前，多小时的任务已经可以用这些前沿模型完成50%的工作量，而80%的时间内完成类似任务则需要略少于一小时。（00:51:06）但这张图表中最令人惊讶的是，它还将之前的所有模型都纳入了对比图表中。这样一来，我们就能清晰地看到技术发展的趋势。这让我非常兴奋的是，如今的产品实际上都是针对模型能够一次处理几分钟任务的场景进行优化的。就连Codex和编程工具，我敢说，它们在命令行界面（CLI）中的交互性设计也充分体现了这一点。（00:51:28）这些产品实际上最多只能支持10分钟左右的任务。我见过有人把Codex推到极限，完成多小时的任务，但这种情况毕竟是少数。不过如果按照这个趋势发展下去，未来12到18个月内，我们可能会看到能够非常连贯地处理多小时测试任务的模型。最终甚至可能实现长达6小时的全天任务，让模型自主执行一段时间。围绕这些模型构建的产品也将焕然一新。你需要给模型提供反馈，显然不能让它完全失控运行一整天。或许有些人会这么做，但大多数人可能不会。这样一来，模型能够处理的任务范围将大大扩展。这正是让我无比期待的未来。（00:52:15）未来12到18个月内，我认为多模态模型的改进也将非常令人兴奋。说到多模态，我主要指的是音频处理。目前模型在音频处理方面已经做得不错，未来6到12个月内，它们在这方面会进一步提升，特别是原生多模态模型，比如语音转语音模型。此外，音频领域，尤其是企业和商业场景中的音频应用，仍然被严重低估。大家都谈论编程，认为它是文本处理，但实际上商业世界中大量活动都是通过音频完成的，许多服务和运营都是通过语音和音频进行的。所以我认为未来12到18个月内，这个领域将变得非常令人兴奋，音频模型应用的潜力也将被进一步释放。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Amazing. So quick summary, expect agents and AI tools to run longer, that trajectory to continue to increase, and then audio and speech becoming a bigger deal, more first party and native and better and core to the experience.
turns.zh: 太棒了。简单总结一下，期待智能助手和AI工具能够持续运行更长时间，相关趋势将继续增强，而音频和语音处理将成为更热门的领域，带来更多第一方和原生模型，以及更出色的核心体验。

turns.speaker: Sherwin Wu
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 是的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Extremely cool. Okay. I want to go back to one of your hot takes, another hot take that I've seen you discuss. You're very bullish on business process automation as an opportunity in the world of AI. Talk about that.
turns.zh: 太酷了。好的。我想回到你的另一个观点，一个我之前就听你讨论过的观点。你对AI时代的业务流程自动化机遇非常乐观。能谈谈这一点吗？

turns.speaker: Sherwin Wu
turns.en: Yeah, this goes back to the thing that I said previously, which is we live in a bubble in Silicon Valley and a lot of the work that we do that we're used to, software engineering, product management, building products is very differently shaped than the work that goes on that runs our entire economy. And I see this day in and day out when I talk to customers. If you talk to any company that's not based in, it's not a tech company, there's a lot of business processes. (00:54:18): And so what I mean by this is, I generally delineate it as software engineering is kind of like open-ended knowledge work, right? And this is why I think tools like Codex tend to be quite good because it's exploring and you're giving it these open-ended things, but software engineering is fundamentally pretty open-ended and is not very repeatable. So you build a feature, you're not trying to build the exact same feature over and over again. (00:54:42): And a lot of tech jobs are in this space. I think data science is kind of in this space as well, even some of the strategic finance stuff. But as you move further and further away from software engineering and like what is core in tech, a lot of jobs are just business processes. They're like repeatable things, repeatable operations that some manager at a company has kind of like iterated on. There's usually a standard operating procedure that people want to do and you don't want to deviate from it that much. In software engineering, the ingenuity is in deviating, but a lot of the work being done in the world is actually just running through these procedures and operations. If I call a support line, they're running through one of these. If I call my utility company, there's a bunch of processes and things that they can and cannot do for me. (00:55:35): And so I'm just extremely bullish on this general category of like... And I think it's underrated because it's so different from what we think about in Silicon Valley, people tend to not think about it, but how can we apply AI and some of the tools and frameworks that we have towards this business process automation, towards automating and making easier repeatable business processes with high determinism that is fully integrated with business data and business decisions and different systems within an enterprise and how can we actually make that process better? Because I actually think there's a lot of opportunity and a lot of work to be done in that area. And we just don't talk about it because it's a little bit less in our wheelhouse.
turns.zh:
是的，这要回到我之前提到的观点——我们生活在硅谷的泡沫中，我们所熟悉的软件工程、产品管理、产品开发等工作模式，与支撑整个经济运行的核心业务流程有着天壤之别。我每天与客户交流时都能深切体会到这一点。若你与非科技公司的企业打交道，就会发现其中蕴含着大量业务流程。（00:54:18）  
我所说的意思是，软件工程本质上属于开放式知识工作，对吧？这也是我认为像Codex这样的工具表现出色的原因——因为它需要不断探索，用户给出开放式任务，而软件工程本质上是高度开放且不可重复的。你开发一个功能时，绝不会重复建造完全相同的功能。（00:54:42）  
许多科技岗位都属于这一范畴。数据科学也属于此类，甚至一些战略财务工作也是如此。但当你逐渐远离软件工程等科技核心领域时，大部分工作就变成了纯粹的业务流程。这些都是可重复的操作流程，企业管理者通常会对其进行优化，通常存在标准操作流程，人们不愿偏离既定模式。软件工程的创新在于打破常规，而现实中大部分工作不过是在执行这些流程和操作。例如，打客服电话时，对方会照本宣科；联系水电公司时，对方能做什么、不能做什么都受流程限制。  
（00:55:35）  
所以我对这一领域极为看好。但人们往往低估了它的价值，因为它与硅谷的认知相去甚远。如何将AI及现有工具框架应用于业务流程自动化，通过高度确定性的流程简化重复性工作，并与企业数据、决策及不同系统深度融合，才是真正的挑战。这一领域蕴藏着巨大机遇和深层挑战，只是我们尚未充分关注，因为它超出了我们的核心专长范围。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So your take here, just to make sure I fully understand it, is you think there's a much bigger opportunity outside of engineering for AI to impact productivity of companies and also jobs of these folks that are doing these kind of repetitive, easily automated tasks?
turns.zh: 所以你的观点是，在工程领域之外，AI对企业生产力和重复性任务自动化影响的潜力要大得多？

turns.speaker: Sherwin Wu
turns.en: Impact jobs and also just impact how work is done. So much of work is done in this way. Basically, I talk to customers all the time, big enterprises, like, "How will AI transform my company? How will it run in a world with AI in 20 years?" And software engineering is part of the story, but there's so much more on the business process side. And I actually think it might look even more different on the business process side and the work there is pretty substantial. (00:57:04): It's actually interesting. I don't know if from an absolute percentage or absolute basis, I don't know if it's bigger or smaller than software engineering. Software is pretty huge and pretty expensive as well, but it is pretty massive and it's definitely bigger than... It's bigger than you would think it is based off of how people talk about it or don't talk about it on X or Twitter.
turns.zh: 它会对就业产生影响，也会改变人们的工作方式。如今很多工作都是以这种方式完成的。基本上，我每天都在和客户沟通，尤其是大型企业客户，他们会问：“人工智能将如何改变我的公司？20年后，在人工智能盛行的世界里，它会如何运作？”软件工程固然是其中一部分，但商业流程方面的影响更为深远。我甚至认为，在商业流程层面，人工智能的影响可能更为显著，而这方面的挑战也相当严峻。（00:57:04）：这确实很有意思。我不确定从绝对比例还是绝对基数来看，人工智能在商业流程方面的影响是否比软件工程更大或更小。软件工程领域规模庞大且成本高昂，但其影响力确实非同寻常，而且规模远超人们的想象——无论是从业者对此的讨论程度，还是在X平台或推特上的相关讨论，都远远不足以体现其重要性。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay. And going in a slightly different direction, having built a platform, building the API, people building on API, the biggest question on people's minds is always just, how do I not have OpenAI squash my idea and build their own thing and then destroy this market I created? What's the general policy, what's the general philosophy of how startups should think about where OpenAI is unlikely to go?
turns.zh: 好的。再换个话题，关于搭建平台、开发API，以及基于API进行开发的公司来说，人们最担心的就是OpenAI会如何窃取他们的创意，开发出自己的产品并颠覆他们所开创的市场。那么，针对初创公司，OpenAI不太可能涉足的领域，普遍的政策和理念是什么？

turns.speaker: Sherwin Wu
turns.en: My general answer here is the market is so big and so massive. I actually think startups should just not overly think about where OpenAI or these labs are going. I've talked to a lot of startups that have not worked out, startups that are doing really well. Every startup that I've seen that is kind of fizzled out is not because OpenAI or a big lab or Google or something has come and squashed them. It's because they built something and it really didn't resonate with the customers. Whereas the ones that take off, even in very competitive spaces like coding, Cursor is huge at this point and it's because they built something that people really love. And so my general advice is like, don't overly stress about this. Just build something that people like and you will have a space in this. (00:58:35): I can't overstate how big of an opportunity there is right now. The opportunity space in building with AI is so big. A good example of this is the space is so big that the Overton window of what is acceptable and not acceptable for VCs to do has completely changed here. VCs are investing in competitive companies left and right. It's just like the space is so big because the opportunity is unlike anything that we've seen before. (00:58:59): And while that affects how VCs operate, from a startup perspective, it's like the most empowering thing in the world because even if you just build something that some people really, really love, you will end up with a massively valuable business. And so that's why I tell people, "Don't overthink about it." The other thing I also think is important to remember, at least from an OpenAI perspective, one thing that we've always held very near and dear, which both Sam and Greg helped reinforce from the top as well, is we actually view ourselves fundamentally as a ecosystem platform company. The API was our first product. (00:59:34): We think it's really important for us to foster this ecosystem and continue to support it and not squash it. And so if you kind of look at the decisions we make, this is all weaved through it. Every single model we've released in one of our products gets released in the API. Even we release these Codex models now that are a little bit more optimized for the Codex harness, but they always find their way into the API and all of our customers end up using those. We don't hold back on any of that. I We think it's really important to keep our platform neutral. And so we don't block competitors. We allow people to have access to our models. We also want, we've recently been testing more of the sign-in with ChatGPT product as well. And so we want to foster this ecosystem. I think it's really important that we do so. (01:00:19): The general thinking about this is a rising tide lifts all boats. And we might be an aircraft carrier. We're pretty big at this point, but we think it's important to raise the tide because everyone kind of benefits and I think we'll benefit as well. Our API itself has grown pretty significantly because we act in this way. And so I'd really encourage people not to view OpenAI as this kind of thing that'll just shove people out of the way, but instead focus on building something valuable. And we remain committed to providing an open ecosystem.
turns.zh:
我的总体回答是，市场规模太大、太广阔了。我认为初创公司不必过度担忧OpenAI或这些实验室的动向。我接触过许多未能成功的初创公司，也有发展得非常好的初创企业。那些最终失败的初创公司，并非因为OpenAI、某个大型实验室或谷歌之类的巨头将它们挤出市场，而是因为他们开发的产品未能真正触动用户需求。而那些成功的公司，比如在编程领域备受瞩目的Cursor，之所以能脱颖而出，是因为他们打造了深受用户喜爱的产品。因此，我的建议是，不要过度焦虑。只要专注于打造人们喜爱的产品，就能在市场中占据一席之地。  

（00:58:35）：我再怎么强调当下机遇的规模之大都不为过。在人工智能领域，机遇空间之广阔令人惊叹。一个典型例子是，VC们投资竞品公司的热情空前高涨，说明这个领域的潜力远超我们以往想象。  

（00:58:59）：虽然VC的运作方式因此发生了变化，但从初创企业的角度来看，这反而是最具赋能性的时刻。即使你只开发出让一小部分人真心喜爱的产品，最终也能收获极具价值的业务。因此我常告诫人们：“别想太多，专注行动。” 

另外，我认为至少从OpenAI的视角来看，有一点至关重要——山姆和格雷格始终强调，我们本质上是一个生态平台公司。API是我们的首个产品。我们深信，培育并支持这个生态系统至关重要，而非压制它。  

举例来说，我们发布的每个模型都会同步到API中。即使现在推出的Codex模型针对Codex Harness进行了优化，最终也会纳入API，让所有用户都能使用。我们从不保留任何技术壁垒，坚持保持平台中立，不阻碍竞争对手获取模型资源。近期我们还在测试与ChatGPT的登录功能，旨在进一步促进生态发展。这对我们至关重要。  

（01:00:19）：整体理念是水涨船高。我们或许是航空母舰，但目前规模已然庞大，却认为提升整个行业水平至关重要，这样大家都能受益，我们自己也会受益。得益于这种开放策略，API用户量显著增长。因此我希望大家不要把OpenAI视为会排挤他人的存在，而是专注于创造有价值的产品。我们将继续致力于构建开放的生态系统。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Why is that important to OpenAI? Just this focus on building a platform, creating a way for people to build businesses? Is that just that's been the vision from the beginning? We want this to be a platform?
turns.zh: 为什么这对OpenAI很重要？仅仅是专注于构建平台，创造让人们建立业务的途径吗？这是否从一开始就是愿景？我们希望这成为一个平台？

turns.speaker: Sherwin Wu
turns.en: It's been the vision from the beginning. It goes back to our charter actually, like our mission. So OpenAI's mission has always been, one, to build AGI, so we're obviously doing that. But then the second thing is to spread the benefits of it to all of humanity. And the main part there is all of humanity. And obviously ChatGPT is trying to do this. We're trying to reach however many, the whole world. But very early on, and this is why we launched the API back in, I think it was like 2020 or something really early. We don't think we as a company will be able to reach all of humanity. I don't know, every corner of the world's pretty deep. And so we actually feel like in order for us to fulfill our mission, we need to have some platform style thing here where we can empower other people to build the customer support bot for podcasters and newsletter hosts because we're not going to be able to do it ourselves. (01:01:58): And so we've largely seen this play out with the API. This is why we talk to so many of our customers and really love seeing the diversity of things built on. But yeah, it's been there since day one because we view it as an expression of our mission.
turns.zh:
这从一开始就是我们的愿景。实际上，这可以追溯到我们的使命宣言。OpenAI的使命一直是，一是开发通用人工智能（AGI），显然我们正在朝着这个方向努力。但第二个目标是让全人类都能享受到其带来的益处。这里关键在于“全人类”。显然，ChatGPT正朝着这个方向努力。我们正努力触达全球用户，但早在很久以前——我想大概是2020年左右——我们就推出了API接口。我们认为，作为一家公司，我们无法独自完成覆盖全人类的任务。毕竟，全球每个角落都深藏着挑战。因此，我们深信，要实现我们的使命，就必须搭建一个平台，让其他人能够开发出针对播客主和新闻通讯主的客户支持机器人——毕竟我们自己无法做到这一点。

（01:01:58）：API接口的成功很好地验证了这一点。正因如此，我们与众多客户保持沟通，乐于看到基于API开发的丰富应用。但从一开始这就是我们的核心理念，因为我们将其视为使命的具体体现。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And you haven't even mentioned the app store that you guys are launching, the ChatGPT app store.
turns.zh: 你们甚至还没提到即将推出的应用商店——ChatGPT应用商店。

turns.speaker: Sherwin Wu
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 是的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Is that under your umbrella, by the way, or is that a different org and team?
turns.zh: 顺便问一下，它归属于你们公司吗？还是属于另一个团队？

turns.speaker: Sherwin Wu
turns.en: It's a different team. So it's under ChatGPT. We obviously collaborate very closely with them. And they built an apps SDK, which was built in close collaboration with our team. But that is more within the ChatGPT umbrella. But that's another example of this. It's like ChatGPT is... We kind of have these 800 million weekly active users who are just coming over and over again. It's a great asset to have as a business, but man would it be better if we could somehow allow other companies to come in and take advantage of this as well and build for this audience as well. And then ultimately, we think it'll help us expand that group as well. And so it all kind of comes back to the mission and we find that being a platform being open tends to help here.
turns.zh: 是另一个团队的。所以它归属于ChatGPT。我们与他们密切合作。他们开发了一个应用SDK，这个SDK是与我们的团队紧密协作完成的。但这更多属于ChatGPT的范畴。不过这也是一个例子。ChatGPT现在有8亿周活用户，不断回访。这对我们来说是宝贵的资产，但如果能让其他公司也利用这一资源，为这些用户群体开发产品，那就再好不过了。最终，我们相信这也能帮助我们扩大用户群体。因此，一切都回归到使命本身，我们发现开放平台往往能在这方面发挥作用。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Just that number, 800 million, I think it's MAs just like-
turns.zh: 就那个数字来说，8亿，应该指的是MAU（月活用户）吧——

turns.speaker: Sherwin Wu
turns.en: No, no, no. It's weekly. Weekly active users.
turns.zh: 不，不，不。是周活用户。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Weekly active.
turns.zh: 周活用户。

turns.speaker: Sherwin Wu
turns.en: Yeah, it's crazy.
turns.zh: 是啊，太疯狂了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Almost a billion people using weekly. It's absurd how these numbers we're just used to now, but that's insane. Unprecedented.
turns.zh: 每周有近10亿人使用。这数字简直太不可思议了。现在我们对这些数字习以为常，但曾经是难以想象的。

turns.speaker: Sherwin Wu
turns.en: Yeah. It's mind-boggling for me to think about from a scale perspective, honestly. And the way I think about it is 10% of the world, and growing, by the way, it's shooting up, come to ChatGPT and use it every day, or sorry, every week.
turns.zh: 是啊。从规模角度来看，这真让人难以置信。说实话，我认为全球10%的人口（而且这个比例还在上升）每天——或者更准确地说，每周——都会使用ChatGPT。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And this point, I just want to double down on this point you're making. OpenAI's mission was to make AI available to all of humanity. And I think some people diss that, they're like, "Oh, it costs money." And the fact that there's a free version of ChatGPT that anybody can use that is not so different from the most powerful AI model that exists in the world for free, that's not gated, that anyone can use. If you're a billionaire, there's only so much more you can get out of AI than what someone in a village in Africa can get. And I know that's always been really important to OpenAI.
turns.zh: 关于这一点，我只想再强调一下您提到的观点。OpenAI的使命是让所有人类都能使用人工智能。我觉得有些人对此不以为然，他们会说：“哦，这需要花钱。”但ChatGPT的免费版本已经上线了，任何人都能使用。它与全球最强大的AI模型相比，免费且无限制，任何人都能使用。如果你是一位亿万富翁，你能从人工智能中获得的收益与非洲村庄里的人相比也相差无几。我知道这一点对OpenAI来说一直非常重要。

turns.speaker: Sherwin Wu
turns.en: Yeah. Yeah. I mean, look, that's why I think we've leaned into the health work, we've leaned into education's going to be very interesting here. The other insane kind of trend here is the free model has gone so smart over time. The free model back in 2022 was good at the time, but it's like nothing compared to what you get today because you get GPT-5 today. And so the raising the floor across the world is kind of something that we're really trying to do. And we view it as part of our mission. (01:04:42): The other flip side of this, by the way, is talking about the billionaires or whatever. I know people love saying you're using the same iPhone that Mark Zuckerberg's probably using or what the billionaires are using, but for like $20 a month, you're basically using the same AI that the billionaires are using. For $200 a month, you get the same pro model that all the billionaires are using, but they're probably not using Pro for everything. They're probably just using the plus tier ones for their day in and day out. And so yeah, this kind of democratization and just spreading of this benefit across all of the world is something that's really meaningful to us and something that drives a lot of what we do.
turns.zh: 是啊。我是说，你看，这就是为什么我们专注于医疗健康领域，教育领域也会非常有趣。另一个令人惊讶的趋势是，免费模型随着时间变得越来越智能。2022年的免费模型当时已经不错，但与现在相比简直不可同日而语，因为现在你能用上GPT-5。所以在全球范围内提升技术水平是我们真正在努力做的事情，我们把这视为我们使命的一部分。（01:04:42）：顺便说一下，关于亿万富翁之类的话题。我知道人们喜欢说你用的iPhone可能和马克·扎克伯格用的一样，或者亿万富翁用的也一样，但每月只需20美元，你就能使用和亿万富翁一样的人工智能模型。每月200美元，你就能获得亿万富翁用的专业版模型，但他们可能不会在所有场景都用专业版。他们日常可能只用增强版。所以是的，这种民主化进程，以及将这种好处推广到全球各地，对我们来说意义非凡，也是我们很多工作的驱动力。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: One last question, just for folks that are thinking about building on the API are just like, "Oh wait, I could do cool stuff with OpenAI's models and APIs." What does your API and platform allow people to do? I know you can build agents on top of the platform. Just talk about what you allow.
turns.zh: 最后一个问题，对于那些考虑在API上进行开发的人，他们可能会说：“哦，等等，我可以用OpenAI的模型和API做一些很酷的事情。”你们的API和平台允许人们做什么？我知道可以在平台上构建智能助手。你能谈谈都允许做些什么吗？

turns.speaker: Sherwin Wu
turns.en: So fundamentally, the API offers a bunch of developer endpoints, and these developer emperors basically let you sample from our models. The most popular one that we have right now is one called Responses API. And so this is an endpoint and it's optimized for building long running agents, so agents that'll work for a while. So what you can basically do is at a very low level, you're basically just giving the model text. The model will work for a while. You can kind of pull it to see what it'll do, and then you'll get the model response back at some point. That's like the lowest level primitive that we have for people. And that's actually what a lot of people use. That's the most popular way of building on top of our API. With that, it is super unopinionated and you can do basically whatever you want. It's like the lowest level thing. (01:06:24): We've also started building more and more layers of abstraction on top to help people build some of these. And so next layer up, we have this thing called the Agents SDK, which has also gotten extremely, extremely popular. This allows you to use the Responses API or some other API endpoints that we have to build what you might more traditionally think of as an agent, like an AI working in an infinite loop. It might have sub-agents that it delegates to. It starts building all this framework, all the scaffolding actually. We'll see where this all goes, but it makes it a lot easier for you to build these kind of agents, giving it guardrails, allowing it to farm out sub-tasks to other agents and kind of orchestrate a swarm of agents. The Agents SDK allows you to do that. (01:07:08): And then above that, we've now started building tools to help also with the meta level of deploying an agent. So we have this product called AgentKit and widgets, which are basically a bunch of UI components that you can use to very easily build a very beautiful UI on top of either our API or Agents SDK because a lot of times these agents look very similar from a UI perspective. And so there's AgentKit. We also have a smattering of evals products, like an evals API where if you want to test and see if your agent or your workflow's working, you can test it in a very quantitative way using our evals product. (01:07:50): And so yeah, I view it as these various layers. They're all kind of helping you build what you want with our AI, with our models, and with increasing levels of abstraction and how opinionated it is. And so you can use the whole stack and it very quickly allows you to build an agent, or you can go down the stack as low as you want to basically Responses API and build whatever you want because of how low low level it is.
turns.zh:
简而言之，API提供了许多开发者端点，这些开发者端点基本上允许你从我们的模型中进行抽样。目前我们最受欢迎的API是名为"响应API"的端点。这个端点专为构建长期运行的智能体而优化，即能够长时间工作的智能体。基本上，用户可以在非常低的层级上直接向模型提供文本，模型会持续运行一段时间。你可以随时查看模型的输出结果，最终会收到模型的响应。这是我们为开发者提供的最基础的原始功能，也是很多人最常用的构建方式。它极其灵活，几乎可以随心所欲地进行开发，是最底层的原始功能。  

（01:06:24）我们还开始在此基础上构建越来越多的抽象层，帮助开发者完成相关工作。例如，下一层是名为"智能体SDK"的工具，它也极受欢迎。该SDK允许你使用响应API或其他API端点来构建传统意义上的智能体——比如一个无限循环的AI。智能体可能包含子智能体，负责分派任务。它会构建整个框架和支撑体系。我们拭目以待，但这确实大大简化了智能体开发过程，提供了安全框架，支持将子任务分派给其他智能体，并实现智能体集群的协同。  

（01:07:08）在此之上，我们还开发了辅助工具，帮助处理智能体部署的元级别问题。例如，名为"AgentKit"的平台和UI组件（widgets），让你可以基于我们的API或智能体SDK轻松构建美观的UI界面，因为很多智能体在UI层面非常相似。还有评估工具（evals API），当你想测试智能体或工作流是否正常运行时，可以通过评估API进行量化测试。  

（01:07:50）总之，我认为这些层级互补。它们都在帮助开发者利用我们的AI和模型进行开发，抽象层次逐渐增加，灵活性也随之增强。你可以使用整个技术栈快速构建智能体，也可以深入底层使用响应API，基于其低层特性自由开发。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Sherwin, is there anything else that you want to share? Anything else you want to leave listeners with? Anything we haven't touched on that you think might be helpful before we get to our very exciting lightning round?
turns.zh: Sherwin，你还有什么想分享的吗？有没有什么想留给听众的信息？在我们进入激动人心的闪电问答环节之前，有没有什么我们没有涉及到但你认为可能有帮助的内容？

turns.speaker: Sherwin Wu
turns.en: The only thing I'd leave folks with is, yeah, I think the next two to three years are going to be some of the most fun in tech and in the startup world that we'll have in a very long time. And I would just encourage people to not take it for granted. I entered the workforce in 2014. It was great for a couple years. I felt like there was a period of five to six years where it wasn't very exciting in tech. And then in the last three years, it's just been the most insanely exciting, energizing period of my career. And I think the next two to three years is going to be a continuation of that. (01:09:01): And so would encourage people not take it for granted, I'm trying to not take it for granted. At some point, this wave's going to play out and it's going to be a lot more incremental, but in the meantime, we're going to get to explore a lot of really cool things, invent a lot of new things and change the world and change how we work. And so that's the main thing I'd leave folks with.
turns.zh:
接下来我想说的是，我认为未来两到三年将是科技和创业领域最激动人心的时期，可能是很长一段时间以来最令人兴奋的时期了。我希望大家不要把这一切视为理所当然。我2014年加入职场，起初几年还不错，但随后有五到六年的时间科技行业并不令人兴奋。过去三年却是最令人激动、最具活力的时期。我相信未来两到三年还会延续这种势头。

（01:09:01）所以我要鼓励大家不要把这一切视为理所当然，我自己也在努力不把它当作理所当然。终有一天，这股浪潮会逐渐平息，发展会更加循序渐进，但在此期间，我们将有机会探索许多酷炫的事物，发明许多新技术，改变世界，改变我们的工作方式。这就是我想传达给大家最重要的信息。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love this message. I want to spend a little more time on it. When you say don't miss it, what do you recommend people do? Is it just build, lean in, learn, join a company building really interesting things? What's your advice to folks that are like, "Okay, I don't want to miss the boat."
turns.zh: 我很喜欢你的这个观点。想再多聊聊。你建议人们怎么做？是专注投入、不断学习、加入正在开发有趣项目的公司吗？对于那些想"不愿错过良机"的人，你有什么建议？

turns.speaker: Sherwin Wu
turns.en: Yeah, I would just say engage with it. So it's basically like what you said, lean in. Building tools on top of this is part of the story. Just using the tools, you don't need to be a software engineer to lean into this. I think a lot of jobs are going to change here. So just using the tools, understanding the limitations of what it can and cannot do so that you can kind of watch the trend of what it can start to do as the models improve. And so it's basically getting used to this technology and getting familiar with it instead of laying back and letting it pass you.
turns.zh: 是的，我想说的是积极参与。这和你的建议基本一致，就是专注投入。基于现有技术进行开发是其中的一个部分。即便你不是软件工程师，也能参与其中。我认为很多工作岗位都会发生变化。所以只要掌握这些工具，理解其局限性，当模型不断改进时，就能见证它能做什么。关键在于熟悉这项技术，而不是被动等待它从你身边溜走。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: On the flip side of that, there's a lot of, I think, stress and just anxiety around, "There's so much happening, how do I keep up? I got to learn Clawdbot this week. Oh God." Is there something you learned about it just not... You're at the center of this. How do you not get overly stressed and worried about missing things that are going on and just you stay on top of news? What are some things you've done and learned?
turns.zh: 反过来说，人们也感到压力重重、焦虑不安，"变化太快，我该如何跟上？这周又要学Clawdbot了，天哪。"你自己处于行业核心，有没有什么方法避免过度焦虑，掌握最新动态？你做了哪些努力？

turns.speaker: Sherwin Wu
turns.en: Yeah. So I think I'm personally a bad example of this because I'm basically chronically online on X and our company Slack. So I actually try and absorb. I end up absorbing a lot of it. What I will say though, just from observing other folks who are less addicted to this stuff like I am. Yeah, a lot of it is noise. You don't need to have 110% of this kind of pass your mind, go into your mind. Honestly, just leaning into one or two different tools, starting small is already more than you need. (01:11:02): Here, I think just the combination of the frenetic pace of the industry, X as a product just creates this insane pace of news, which is honestly very overwhelming. The main thing is you don't need to know all of that to really engage with what's happening right now. And even something as simple as just like install the Codex Cline and play around with it. Install ChatGPT and connect it to a couple of your internal data sources, Notion, Slack, GitHub, and see what it can and cannot do. All of that I think is a part of it.
turns.zh: 是的。我个人在这方面做得不好，因为我基本上一整天都在X和公司的Slack上刷信息。所以我尽量吸收信息。但从观察其他不那么沉迷这些平台的人来看，他们也面临很多噪音。没必要全盘接受所有信息。专注一两个工具，从小处着手就足够了。（01:11:02）我觉得关键在于，行业的快节奏加上X这样的产品，带来了海量信息，这确实让人应接不暇。但要参与当下的事务，真的不需要了解所有信息。哪怕只是安装Codex Clone，尝试一下，安装ChatGPT，将其与内部数据源（Notion、Slack、GitHub）连接起来，看看它能做什么、不能做什么，这些都是很好的入门方式。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Amazing. Sherwin, with that we've reached our very exciting lightning round. I've got five questions for you. Are you ready?
turns.zh: 太棒了。谢尔温，接下来我们要进行激动人心的闪电问答环节了。我有五个问题要问你。你准备好了吗？

turns.speaker: Sherwin Wu
turns.en: Yeah. Yeah, absolutely.
turns.zh: 好的。好的，没问题。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: First question, what are two or three books that you find yourself recommending most to other people?
turns.zh: 第一个问题：你觉得哪两三本书是你最常向别人推荐的？

turns.speaker: Sherwin Wu
turns.en: I'll talk about one nonfiction and one fiction book. The fiction book was I just finished reading it. I really recommend it. There Is No Antimemetics Division by qntm. I think it's like an online author, but I saw it being shared on X. It's like a science fiction-y kind of book and I basically devoured it in like two days. It's super, super well written, super fascinating. It's about a government agency that's fighting things that make you forget it. And so it's just a very smart creative book and fresh, honestly, in terms of source material that I really like. So I'd recommend that one. The book is also unintentionally hilarious. So it's meant to be this sci-fi, almost like horror style book, but it made me laugh a couple times. So that's the fiction book. (01:12:43): Non-fiction, so I'm going to cheat and I'm going to recommend two of them. So in the last year, I've been reading a lot more about China and the US-China relations. And I think there are two books that came out in the last year that have been really, really eye-opening for me in that regard. First one is the Dan Wang book, Breakneck. That one was really, really good. I really liked his analogy of the lawyerly, US is the lawyerly society, China is the engineering society, and there are pros and cons to each. I read it and I was like, hmm, yeah, it does seem like we're run by lawyers in the US. So then that's one. (01:13:14): And the other one is the Patrick McGee book on Apple in China. It was super, super interesting. I'm a huge Apple fanboy. If you could see my desk right now, it's all Apple stuff. But just one, it was just super fascinating learning about Apple's relationship to China. And then two, it just had a lot of inside information about Apple as a company that I found fascinating. So it was also quite a page-turner and also a very, very timely book as well.
turns.zh: 我要说一本非小说类书籍和一本小说类书籍。小说类书籍是我刚读完的，非常推荐。是qntm写的《没有反记忆部门》。我觉得这本书作者是个网络作家，但我在X上看到有人分享。这是一本带有科幻色彩的书，我两天就读完了。写得非常非常好，特别引人入胜。讲的是一个政府机构对抗让人遗忘事物的东西。整体来说这是一本非常有创意、很新颖的书，尤其是在素材选取方面，我很喜欢。所以我推荐这本。还有这本书无意中特别搞笑。本来是部科幻、近乎恐怖风格的书，但让我笑了好几次。这就是小说类书籍。（01:12:43）非小说类书籍，我要偷个懒，推荐两本。过去一年我读了很多关于中美关系的书，觉得去年有两本让我大开眼界。第一本是王丹的《急转直下》。这本书真的很棒。我很喜欢他用律师社会和工程社会来比喻中美两国，各自有利弊。我读完后就觉得，嗯，是啊，我们美国确实是律师社会。第二本是麦吉写的《苹果在中国的故事》。特别有意思。我是苹果的超级粉丝，如果你现在能看到我的书桌，全是苹果相关的东西。但这本书特别有意思，一是讲苹果和中国的关系，二是里面有很多苹果内部信息，非常吸引人。所以这本书也特别引人入胜，也是本很应时的书。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: The antimemetics book sounds amazing. I'm buying it right now as you're talking.
turns.zh: 那本反记忆部门听起来很棒。我现在就去买。

turns.speaker: Sherwin Wu
turns.en: Yeah. Yeah. I think it's only a couple hundred pages. I literally finished it in two days.
turns.zh: 是啊是啊。这本书才几百页，我两天就读完了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Perfect. The dream.
turns.zh: 太完美了。梦想成真。

turns.speaker: Sherwin Wu
turns.en: It was just so, so good.
turns.zh: 真的太棒了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay. Great tip. Okay. Favorite recent movie or TV show you have really enjoyed?
turns.zh: 好的。好建议。好的。最近有没有特别喜欢的电影或电视剧？

turns.speaker: Sherwin Wu
turns.en: Yeah, that one's tough because I have two kids and a busy job, and so I really haven't had much time to watch TV shows. I will say in the last couple weeks, I watched a couple episodes. I'm actually a big anime guy. And so I watched a couple episodes. There's a new season of this anime called Jujutsu Kaisen that's out. So season three of JJK was really good. In general, I'm a huge fan of Japanese anime. I think they create the most novel and unique plots and universes that Western media has shied away from. And so generally a big fan of that. But yeah, haven't really watched much, but saw a couple episodes of JJK recently.
turns.zh: 嗯，这个问题挺难的，因为我有两个孩子，工作又忙，所以没太多时间看电视剧。不过最近几周我看了几集动漫。我特别喜欢动漫。最近新出的《咒术回战》第三季特别好。我总体上很喜欢日本动漫，觉得他们创造了很多西方媒体避之不及的、新奇独特的剧情和宇宙。所以特别喜欢动漫。不过确实最近没怎么看，但最近看了几集《咒术回战》。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Extremely understandable in your role.
turns.zh: 在你这个角色中，这完全可以理解。

turns.speaker: Sherwin Wu
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 是啊。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Favorite product you recently discovered that you really love.
turns.zh: 你最近发现的最喜欢的产品是什么？

turns.speaker: Sherwin Wu
turns.en: Yeah. Okay. So I recently had to set up a wifi and like home networking and I went all-in on Ubiquiti routers and security cameras. I'd never heard of it before I had to do this. I always just had a very simple setup. And it is just such a well-built product. I don't know if you used it before, but it's basically like the Apple of home networking. So beautiful products, but the thing that actually makes it extremely good is its software is good. And so they have a really great mobile app to help manage all of the home networking. (01:15:19): And so basically Ubiquiti, you can use it to buy wireless routers. You need ethernet wiring throughout your house to use it. But I actually think what makes it really good are its security cameras. So if you have security cameras that are plugged into the Ubiquiti ecosystem, they have an incredible mobile app and Apple TV app and iPad app to kind of see the live feed of your cameras. And so they're a little pricey, but not that pricey, but it's been just an incredible product experience.
turns.zh: 是啊，好的。我最近需要设置Wi-Fi和家庭网络，所以就全力投入了Ubiquiti路由器和安防摄像头。我之前从没听说过这个品牌，以前用的都是很简单的配置。Ubiquiti的产品做工真是太棒了。不知道你用过没，它简直就是家庭网络领域的苹果。产品设计精美，但真正出色的还是软件。他们的移动应用能帮你管理整个家庭网络。（01:15:19）Ubiquiti的路由器需要全屋布线才能使用，但我觉得安防摄像头才是亮点。只要摄像头接入Ubiquiti生态系统，配套的移动应用、Apple TV应用和iPad应用就能实时查看监控画面。虽然价格不算便宜，但整体体验堪称惊艳。

turns.en: All right. I went eero, so I made a mistake.

turns.speaker: Sherwin Wu
turns.en: Yeah. The one that I always repeat to myself is never feel sorry for yourself. There's a lot of things that are going to happen at work, in life, and reminding yourself to never feel sorry and that you always have a sense of agency to kind of pull yourself up is something that I've had to tell myself a lot and also something that I repeat to a lot of other folks as well.
turns.zh: 有啊。我常对自己说永远别自怨自艾。工作和生活中总会遇到各种事，要提醒自己别自怜自艾，保持积极进取的心态，这句话我常对自己说，也常跟别人分享。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Last question. So in your previous life, you worked at Opendoor where you led work on basically figuring out how much to pay for houses. You basically built a model that told the company, "Here's how much we'll pay for this house." What's a variable in the price of a house that you didn't expect is really important and impacts the price of a house?
turns.zh: 最后一个问题。你之前在Opendoor工作，负责房屋估价模型的开发。能否谈谈一个意外发现的房屋估价变量？

turns.speaker: Sherwin Wu
turns.en: There's a bunch that were surprising. I'll maybe list the couple of the most interesting ones. Power lines and high voltage power lines are super, super, they actually impact your price quite a lot. I didn't really fully internalize this until I went to Dallas and observed when your house sits next to one of these giant voltage lines, it was buzzing and most people have families, you don't want your kids near there. So I think that was one that really, really kind of surprised me.
turns.zh: 有很多意外发现。比如高压电线对房价影响巨大。我去达拉斯实地考察后，才深刻体会到当房子紧邻高压电线时，电线嗡嗡作响，附近住户大多不愿让孩子靠近。这真让我大吃一惊。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That makes sense.
turns.zh: 有道理。

turns.speaker: Sherwin Wu
turns.en: Yeah. And then the other one, which was something that was always something really difficult for us to quantify was floor plans. And so it is very important. Yes, of course it's really important, but just quantifying what a good floor plan is like and what a really bad floor plan is like. We were doing all these things with how wide is the kitchen and what style of kitchen is it and then where's the master bedroom? And so it was just really, really hard to quantify. But I remember floor plan was a big one because we'd have a home that wouldn't sell and then our ops team would go in and be like, yeah, it's the floor plan issue. So how could you tell? You go inside, you just feel it. The floor plan feels off. (01:17:50): So yeah, those were ones that were surprising. And then the last one that was more impactful than I thought is general curb appeal and even the front door. And so I actually think there's a Zillow book on this where the front door placement tends to be the highest ROI for homes, but just the feel of like as you walk up to the home as a buyer, what you're interacting with and the first moments of the house, I think I'd underrated its importance.
turns.zh: 是的。还有另一件对我们来说一直很难量化的事情，就是户型图。这真的非常重要。没错，户型图确实很重要，但要量化一个好的户型是什么样的，一个糟糕的户型又是什么样的，却很难。我们会做各种分析，比如厨房有多宽，厨房是什么风格，主卧室在哪里之类的。但量化这些真的太难了。不过我记得户型图是个关键问题，因为有些房子卖不出去时，我们的运营团队就会说，问题出在户型图上。所以你怎么判断呢？你走进房子里，自己就能感觉到。户型感觉不对劲。（01:17:50）：所以是的，这些都让人很意外。最后一个比我想象中更有影响力的是整体外观吸引力，甚至是前门。所以我记得Zillow有一本书提到，前门的位置往往是房屋的最高投资回报率。但当买家走近房子时，他们与房屋的首次互动，以及最初的印象，我觉得我低估了它的重要性。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That is extremely interesting. And I love that you had to figure how to do all this in code and not walking around look at these houses.
turns.zh: 这真是太有趣了。而且我很高兴你不得不把所有这些工作用代码实现，而不是亲自去看这些房子。

turns.speaker: Sherwin Wu
turns.en: Yeah. And then floor plans. I have a bunch of stories around floor plans, it's not digitized so there's like a handful of people who have paper floor plans of all these homes in Phoenix and Dallas. Yeah, a lot of fun stories from the Opendoor days.
turns.zh: 是的。还有户型图。我有很多关于户型图的故事，它们没有数字化，所以只有少数几个人手里有凤凰城和达拉斯所有房子的纸质户型图。是的，OpenDoor时期有很多有趣的故事。
